column4: A small unit sacrificed or eaten makes an attacker that strikes twice bigger; most other pairs are generic "both buff" or hit the player, and Curse of Wrath (damage) and Immortal Trade (heal) are not really grows.
A unit that dies comes back from the discard pile to hand and grows each time; the rest only share a set or a generic play/move link.
Healing a damaged unit makes another unit grow (Lightchaser, Vitality/Armor builders); heals tag is correct here.
A unit eats or feeds on a small friendly unit and gains its strength and defence; most links are generic "more health".
Pull enemy units into neighbouring cells so a damage card splashes or a forced attack hits the neighbour; several pairs only damage the player (no player health).
A unit destroys your own units when it attacks and another brings them back from the discard pile; the rest are set-only links.
Sacrificing a unit pays for an attacker while a unit nearby grows or summons when a unit dies; positional and player-damage pairs fail.
The few true pairs are sacrifice or damage combos, not extra defence; links are mostly "both buff" or hit the player, tags fit poorly.
True pairs are sacrifice-for-death-effect or lifesteal-heal combos that have nothing to do with few big units; tags wrong for the pairing.
Only pulling enemies together before a hit-all-around works; the rest hit the player or are tribal or set-only links.
No pair cuts the cost of a damage unit; links are generic "is played", "makes units die" or player damage.
Returning a unit to hand so its on-play damage goes off again when replayed; player-damage and exhaust pairs fail.
Destroying your own unit whose death effect, or an enemy death, gives extra supply; many pairs are set-only or a generic "pays for it".
Destroy a unit, then bring it back from the discard pile (or onto your side); the rest share only a set.
Destroying your own units outright sets off their on-death effects or feeds a unit that counts deaths.

A second resource (coins) pays for another card's fee, or units gaining strength earn extra supply; most "many" tags here are wrong (Shivers, Boris, Spirit of the Wild are not area effects) and "pays for it" links are generic.
Area damage rarely feeds return effects: it hits enemy units while back cards revive your own; only a unit that returns stronger after dying (Ouroboros) works.
Area damage on your own lane kills your units with death effects (summon on death, draw on death, kill an enemy on death).

Mostly generic "more supply pays for a damage spell"; real cases are extra supply raising an X-cost spell or enemy deaths granting supply, and Collusion/Dark Crystal tags look wrong (player life, not unit damage).
A cost cut on spells in a lane, or moving enemies together before an area spell; several spelldmg tags mean hitting the player (Corporeal Cadence, Choke), which has no Three Bases meaning.
A spell that refunds its own supply (or refills supply and draws) sets off spell-cast rewards for free.
Casting spells makes a unit cheaper, or a free spell sets off a cast reward; most other links are just "it is a spell", and Three Wishes is tagged spellpay but is a cost cut.
Cards that create spells in hand feed cast rewards (one cast reward per created spell); the rest is the generic "it is a spell".
Copy/tutor effects rarely feed cast rewards beyond being a spell; only a spell that returns a copy of itself to hand or discard repeats the reward.
Extra supply raises an X cost, or a second resource and its cost cut work together; many links are just "more supply pays for it".
Returning a unit that steals supply on play replays it, or a unit that comes back after dying lets a "gain supply if it dies" effect repeat.
Sacrificing your own unit for supply also sets off that unit's death effect (buff, summon on death, more resource).
A death effect that draws units of the same kind that another card already made cheaper, or a sacrifice that cuts a unit's cost; most links share only a set.
Cost cuts and copy/tutor effects almost never interact; the links are set-mates or anti-synergy (Loki and Gorgon).
Returning a unit to hand replays its on-play cost cut, or a card kept in hand at round end gets cheaper.
A spell or card that plays a unit sets off a unit that triggers on spells or on being played; few pairs are about cost cuts or big units, so both tags look wrong for most cards.
Return your own unit to hand so its on-play effect goes off again; the draw-from-deck pairs are generic.
Return a unit to hand to replay its on-play copy effect, or keep a card in hand that grows while kept; most "fills your hand" links are generic.
A unit that dies returns to hand or discards cheaper, or a card kills your own units for their death effects; the hit-enemy and player-life pairs fail.
Sacrifice your own unit, then bring it back from the discard pile; many pairs damage enemies, not your own units, so the bring-back never fires.
Return a healer to hand to replay its heal; most heals tags mean player or hero life or artifact repair, which Three Bases has no use for.
A defence boost lets a unit survive damage and return to hand, or a unit with a death buff is killed on purpose; the deck-play pairs are generic.
Only a unit that comes back when destroyed by a card's text pairs with a bring-back; the rest share a set or rely on player life.
A spell that returns to your deck keeps feeding a unit that grows on each spell cast; most tall tags and links are generic.
A cheap short-lived unit dies or is sacrificed and feeds a card that pays out or costs less per own unit death; many links are just "kills it".
A heal that also burns out a unit kills it for a death or death-count effect; most pairs are placement-only and the heals tag often means player life.
Damage or destroy your own unit that comes back when destroyed by text; guard and shield cards rarely care about sacrifices.
Sacrifice cheap fodder to summon or grow a big unit, or a big unit eats its neighbours for strength; the placement links fail.
A heal or vitality on your unit sets off a unit that gains strength or defence whenever it is healed; the move and placement pairs fail.
